6	
7	# Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100)
8	
9	ASD-STE100 is a controlled-language standard built by the aerospace and defense industry (ASD, the AeroSpace and Defense Industries Association of Europe) to stop maintenance technicians from misreading English instructions. The standard removes the two biggest sources of misreading: words with more than one meaning, and sentences with more than one possible structure.
10	
11	This skill borrows that same discipline for a different reader: an **AI agent or a downstream system** that has to parse an English string — an error message, a tool description, an inter-agent instruction, a status report — without a human in the loop to resolve ambiguity. If a maintenance technician can misread "close the valve" as an adjective ("the valve that is near") instead of a command, so can a language model.
12	
13	## When to Use This Skill
14	
15	- An agent's output (explanation, instruction, log message, tool description) reads as dense, jargon-heavy, or ambiguous.
16	- Text will be consumed by another agent, a translation pipeline, or a non-native English reader, and misparsing has a real cost.
17	- You are writing a prompt, system message, or tool description and want to remove ambiguity before a model ever sees it.
18	- You want a **before/after** comparison showing exactly which rule was violated and how the rewrite fixes it. Ask for it — the default output is the rewritten text alone (see Output Format).
19	
20	This skill is not for creative or marketing copy — STE is deliberately flat and literal. Do not apply it to text where voice, nuance, or persuasion is the point.
21	
22	## Two Modes
23	
24	Pick a mode before rewriting. If the user does not say which, infer it from the text type. Keep the choice internal unless the user asks for the rule table (see Output Format).
25	
26	**Strict** — procedures, error messages, tool and function descriptions, inter-agent instructions, safety text. Anywhere a wrong reading has a cost. Apply every rule below, including the hard length caps and one-word-one-meaning discipline.
27	
28	**STE-flavored** — READMEs, PR descriptions, changelogs, explanatory prose. Apply the structural rules in full and treat the lexical rules as advisory (see Core Rewrite Rules for that split). In practice that means keeping the sentence length caps, active voice, simple tenses, no phrasal verbs, no semicolons, no nominalization and no marketing adjectives, while dropping the one-word-one-meaning lockdown: prose needs some range, and a strict rewrite of prose reads as a personality transplant rather than a clarification.
29	
30	The two modes and the structural/lexical split are the same distinction seen from two directions. The split says which rules this skill can verify without ASD's dictionary. The modes say which of them to enforce for a given kind of text.
31	
32	## Source and Scope
33	
34	This skill encodes the **rule categories** of ASD-STE100 Issue 9 (Jan 2025): 53 writing rules across 9 sections covering word choice, grammar, sentence structure, and style, backed by a dictionary of ~900 approved words (one meaning, one part of speech each) and ~1,200 words to avoid with suggested replacements. See `references/writing-rules.md` for the full rule summary and citations.
35	
36	It does **not** reproduce ASD's ~900-word approved dictionary verbatim. ASD-STE100 is free to obtain, but it is not free to redistribute: Issue 9, page 2 states that "no reproduction or publication of it, in whole or in part, shall be made without the written authority of an officer of ASD," and grants free reproduction rights only to eight listed categories (ASD/AIA/AIAC member associations and their member companies and customers, member-state defence ministries, A4A, airworthiness authorities, and universities and research institutes for educational purposes). This project is in none of them, so the dictionary stays out of this repo.
37	
38	Instead, this skill applies the *underlying principle* (pick the plainest, most common word available and use it the same way every time) rather than checking against a fixed word list. When exact ASD-approved wording matters (e.g. actual aircraft maintenance documentation), get the standard and check word-by-word against the real dictionary. Request it from the [official downloads page](https://www.asd-ste100.org/STE_downloads.html) — note that this is a request form that emails you a link, not a direct download.
39	
40	## Core Rewrite Rules
41	
42	STE's rules divide into two kinds, and this skill can only fully deliver one of them. **Structural rules** are self-contained: they describe sentence shape, and you can apply them from the description alone. **Lexical rules** are defined entirely by the official ~900-word dictionary, which this skill deliberately does not reproduce (see Source and Scope). Without that dictionary, the lexical rules degrade from a checkable standard into a preference for plain words.
43	
44	Apply the structural rules with confidence. Apply the lexical rules as a direction of travel, and say so in your output rather than implying dictionary compliance you cannot verify.
45	
46	### Structural rules — apply these
47	
48	| Rule | Do | Don't |
49	|---|---|---|
50	| Active voice | "The agent deletes the file." | "The file is deleted (by the agent)." — unless the actor is genuinely unknown or irrelevant |
51	| No phrasal verbs (Rule 9.3) | "Remove the panel." / "Start the job." | "Take off the panel." / "Spin up the job." — a two-word verb has meanings the parts do not predict |
52	| One instruction per sentence | "Open the file. Read line 3." | "Open the file and read line 3, then check if it matches." |
53	| Sentence length | ≤20 words for instructions/procedures, ≤25 words for descriptions | Long compound/subordinate-clause sentences |
54	| No semicolons (Rule 8.1) | Split into separate sentences | Any semicolon at all — STE bans the mark outright, not only as a clause join. (Rule 8.1 permits every other standard punctuation mark. The em dash is *not* banned by STE, though it often signals a sentence that should be split.) |
55	| Noun clusters | ≤3 words stacked as a noun phrase ("fuel pump valve") | 4+ word noun stacks ("high pressure fuel pump inlet valve assembly") |
56	| No ellipsis | Keep the subject, verb, and article explicit even if it reads longer | Drop words to save space ("Files not backed up will be lost" → ambiguous which files) |
57	| Keep modality | "The request **may have** failed." stays "may have" | Promote a hedge to a fact ("The request failed.") or invent a certainty the source did not state |
58	| Paragraph limits | One topic per paragraph, ≤6 sentences | Multi-topic paragraphs |
59	| Lists for sequences | Use a numbered or bulleted list for 3+ steps or conditions | Bury a sequence inside one prose sentence |
60	
61	### Lexical rules — direction of travel only
62	
63	| Rule | Do | Don't | Why it is weaker here |
64	|---|---|---|---|
65	| One word, one meaning | Pick one verb for one action and reuse it every time (e.g. always "check", never mix "check"/"verify"/"confirm" for the same action) | Rotate synonyms for the same idea across a document | Consistency within a document is checkable. Which word is the *approved* one is not, without the dictionary. |
66	| One part of speech per word | "Apply oil to the valve" (oil = noun) | "Oil the valve" (oil = verb) | Whether "oil" is approved as a noun only is a dictionary fact. Prefer the noun form when both read equally well. Do not claim compliance. |
67	| Verb, not noun (Rule 3.7) | "Analyze the log." | "Perform an analysis of the log." — a noun form of an action makes the sentence longer and hides who acts | Rule 3.7 says "use an **approved** verb to describe an action." Preferring the verb form is safe to apply anywhere. Knowing which verb is the approved one needs the dictionary. |
68	| Domain terms | Keep necessary technical nouns/verbs, but define them once if not common English (STE allows a project-specific glossary beyond its base dictionary) | Use jargon without ever defining it | The glossary allowance is real STE, but the base dictionary it extends is absent. |
69	
70	### Simple tenses — apply with one exception
71	
72	STE permits infinitive, imperative, simple present, simple past, simple future, and past participle as adjective. It excludes present perfect and other compound forms: "we received the report", not "we have received the report".
73	
74	Aircraft manuals never need present perfect, so the exclusion costs the standard nothing. Other text is not always so lucky. "The job has completed" (and its output is available now) and "the job completed" (at some past point) are different statements, and status text frequently needs the first. **Where the compound form carries information the simple form cannot — current relevance, or a hedge as in "may have failed" — keep it and flag the departure.** Elsewhere, follow the rule.
75	
76	## Scan Checklist
77	
78	These six habits cover most of what makes machine-written English hard to parse. Each one is mechanical: you can point at the exact word or punctuation mark that breaks the rule, with no judgment call. Scan for all six before you rewrite anything.
79	
80	1. **Synonym rotation** — the same thing gets several names in one document ("the user", "the customer", "the client"). The reader cannot tell whether they are one thing or three. Fix: pick one name, use it every time.
81	2. **Hedge stacking** — helper verbs and qualifiers pile up until the sentence asserts nothing ("it is important to note that this may potentially help to improve"). Fix: state the claim, or delete it.
82	3. **Nominalization** — an action frozen into a noun ("perform an analysis of", "provides assistance to"). Fix: use the verb ("analyze", "helps").
83	4. **Marketing adjectives** — words that claim quality instead of showing it: seamless, robust, powerful, cutting-edge, effortless, blazing-fast. Fix: delete, or replace with the measurement that earns the claim.
84	5. **Run-on sentences** — several ideas joined by semicolons or em dashes. Fix: one idea per sentence.
85	6. **Soft phrasal verbs** — spin up, reach out, dive into, kick off. Fix: use the single plain verb (start, contact, read, begin).
86	
87	## Process
88	
89	1. Pick the mode (Strict or STE-flavored). Say which only when the user asked for the rule table — see Output Format.
90	2. Read the input text once for meaning — do not start rewriting before you understand what it must still say afterward.
91	3. Walk it sentence by sentence. Flag every rule violation from the Core Rewrite Rules tables and every habit from the Scan Checklist. In STE-flavored mode, flag the lexical rules but do not enforce them. For a mechanical first pass over the structural rules, run `scripts/ste-lint.py` (stdin or file args, `--json` for structured output); it checks semicolons, sentence length, phrasal verbs, nominalization, marketing adjectives, synonym rotation, dangling-conjunction in supported list items, passive voice, and compound tenses, and by design never flags hedges or modality. `--baseline N` tolerates N hard violations (for adopting on existing docs); `--disable rule1,rule2` silences named rules.
92	4. Rewrite each flagged sentence to fix the violation while preserving the original meaning exactly. If a rewrite would drop necessary precision (a safety condition, a scope qualifier, a number), keep the longer phrasing and flag it instead of silently simplifying.
93	   - **Check modality before you commit to a rewrite.** Hedges ("may", "could", "sometimes", "is likely to") carry the author's confidence, and confidence is content. A shorter sentence that upgrades a hedge to a fact is not a simplification — it is a different claim. This is the most common way a well-intentioned STE rewrite goes wrong, because hedges are exactly what a length cap tempts you to cut.
94	   - Never add a fact the source did not state. A rewrite that reads better because it supplies a cause, a frequency, or a mechanism has stopped being a rewrite.
95	5. Output the rewritten text (see Output Format). Keep the mode choice and the rule analysis internal unless the user asked to see them.
96	6. If the input already complies, say so — do not force changes onto compliant text.
97	
98	## Output Format
99	
100	**Default: the rewritten text, and nothing else.** Most callers want a result they can paste straight into a tool description, an error string, or a prompt. Print the simplified text on its own. Do not add a preamble about this skill, a mode announcement, a violation count, a summary of what changed, a rule table, or a closing offer to explain further.
101	
102	The one permitted addition: if step 4 kept a longer phrasing on purpose, add a single line after the text, prefixed `Kept as-is:`, naming the phrase and the precision that would have been lost. Omit the line when there is nothing to report.
103	
104	**On request: the rule table.** When the user asks to see the reasoning — "show the diff", "which rules did it break", "explain the changes", "before/after" — output this table instead:
105	
106	```markdown
107	| Rule violated | Original | Simplified |
108	|---|---|---|
109	| Present perfect tense | "We have received your request." | "We received your request." |
110	| Noun cluster (4+ words) | "the agent task queue priority handler" | "the handler that sets task-queue priority" |
111	
112	Mode: Strict. 7 violations found.
113	```
114	
115	Follow the table with a one-line note on anything you deliberately did **not** simplify, and why (usually: simplifying would lose required precision).
116	
117	## Boundaries
118	
119	**Will:**
120	- Rewrite ambiguous or dense English into short, single-meaning, active-voice sentences.
121	- Return the rewritten text alone by default, and name the rules it applied when the user asks.
122	- Preserve every fact, condition, and scope qualifier in the original.
123	- Preserve the strength of every hedge, and add no claim the source did not make.
124	- Suggest a one-line glossary entry for domain terms that must stay.
125	
126	**Will not:**
127	- Reproduce ASD's official ~900-word dictionary as if it were memorized verbatim — always treat the official download as the source of truth for exact approved wording.
128	- Simplify creative, marketing, or persuasive copy where voice and nuance are the point.
129	- Silently drop a safety condition, exception, or scope qualifier to shorten a sentence — it will flag the trade-off instead.
130	- Convert "may have failed" into "failed", or "could be caused by X" into "X is the cause" — losing a hedge changes the claim.
131	- Guarantee an aerospace/defense-grade STE-compliant document. This is a general-purpose clarity tool inspired by STE, not a certified STE authoring tool.
132	- Make weak content true or useful. STE fixes the *form* of a text, not its substance. A hollow paragraph rewritten under these rules becomes a clean, short, well-punctuated hollow paragraph. If the text has nothing to say, no rewrite fixes that — say so instead of polishing it.
133	- Shorten past the point of clarity. Cutting words is not the goal. Removing ambiguity is the goal. Past a certain point compression starts costing the reader time rather than saving it, so stop when the sentence is unambiguous, not when it is shortest.

114	def _sentence_starts(text):

118	    closing quotes or brackets. Known abbreviations do not end a sentence.
119	    One pass over the words keeps the cost linear in the text length.

121	    words = list(re.finditer(r"\S+", text))
122	    if not words:

125	    for word, next_word in zip(words, words[1:]):
126	        end = SENTENCE_END.search(word.group())
127	        if not end:
128	            continue
129	        core = word.group()[:end.start() + 1].lstrip(OPENERS)
130	        if core.lower() in ABBREVIATIONS:
131	            continue
132	        if (DOTTED_ABBREVIATION.fullmatch(core)
133	                and not next_word.group().lstrip(OPENERS)[:1].isupper()):
134	            continue
135	        starts.append(next_word.start())
136	    return starts

144	    once, and each finding points at the line and column where it starts.

146	    offsets, position = [], 0
147	    for _, _, text in pieces:
148	        offsets.append(position)
149	        position += len(text) + 1

158	        offset = offsets[index]

161	                         "col": source_column + start - offset + 1,
162	                         "rule": "long-sentence", "level": "advisory-free",
163	                         "match": f"{n} words",
164	                         "message": f"Sentence has {n} words (cap {MAX_WORDS}). Split it."})

181	    """Return trimmed table cells and their zero-based source columns.
182	
183	    A pipe must separate at least two cells. Escaped pipes stay in their cell.
184	    This deliberately implements only the ordinary Markdown table shape; it is
185	    enough to distinguish a table from prose that happens to contain a pipe.
186	    """
187	    left = len(line) - len(line.lstrip())
188	    right = len(line.rstrip())
189	    content = line[left:right]
190	    if "|" not in content:
191	        return None
192	    if content.startswith("|"):
193	        content = content[1:]
194	        left += 1
195	    if content.endswith("|"):
196	        content = content[:-1]
197	    raw_cells = re.split(r"(?<!\\)\|", content)
198	    if len(raw_cells) < 2:
199	        return None
200	
201	    cells = []
202	    column = left
203	    for raw_cell in raw_cells:
204	        leading = len(raw_cell) - len(raw_cell.lstrip())
205	        cells.append((raw_cell.strip(), column + leading))
206	        column += len(raw_cell) + 1
207	    return cells

210	def _markdown_table_cells(lines):
211	    """Map ordinary Markdown table rows to their prose cells.
212	
213	    The separator row anchors detection, so pipe-containing prose is not
214	    treated as a table. Both leading-pipe and no-leading-pipe table styles are
215	    accepted when their header and body use the same number of cells.
216	    """
217	    table_cells = {}
218	    index = 1
219	    while index < len(lines):
220	        separator = _split_table_row(lines[index])
221	        header = _split_table_row(lines[index - 1])
222	        if (not separator or not header or len(separator) != len(header)
223	                or not all(TABLE_SEPARATOR_CELL.fullmatch(cell)
224	                           for cell, _ in separator)):
225	            index += 1
226	            continue
227	
228	        table_cells[index - 1] = header
229	        table_cells[index] = []
230	        index += 1
231	        while index < len(lines):
232	            row = _split_table_row(lines[index])
233	            if not row or len(row) != len(separator):
234	                break
235	            table_cells[index] = row
236	            index += 1
237	    return table_cells

240	def _dangling_conjunction_findings(text, filename):
241	    lines = text.splitlines()
242	    findings = []
243	    in_fence = False
244	    index = 0
245	    while index < len(lines):
246	        line = lines[index]
247	        stripped = line.strip()
248	        if CODE_FENCE.match(stripped):
249	            in_fence = not in_fence
250	            index += 1
251	            continue
252	        if in_fence:
253	            index += 1
254	            continue
255	        start = LIST_ITEM_START.match(line)
256	        if not start:
257	            index += 1
258	            continue
259	
260	        content_indent = (len(start.group("indent"))
261	                          + len(start.group("marker"))
262	                          + len(start.group("gap")))
263	        item_lines = [(index, start.group("body"))]
264	        next_index = index + 1
265	        item_fence = False
266	        while next_index < len(lines):
267	            candidate = lines[next_index]
268	            candidate_stripped = candidate.strip()
269	            if CODE_FENCE.match(candidate_stripped):
270	                # Fence delimiters are state markers, not meaningful item lines.
271	                item_fence = not item_fence
272	                next_index += 1
273	                continue
274	            if item_fence:
275	                next_index += 1
276	                continue
277	            if not _is_list_continuation(candidate, content_indent):
278	                break
279	            item_lines.append((next_index, candidate))
280	            next_index += 1
281	
282	        meaningful = []
283	        for line_index, item_line in item_lines:
284	            # Preserve code spans as neutral operands while ignoring their contents.
285	            cleaned = INLINE_CODE.sub(" CODE ", item_line).strip()
286	            if cleaned:
287	                meaningful.append((line_index, cleaned))
288	        if meaningful:
289	            end_line_index, end_line = meaningful[-1]
290	            conjunction = CONJUNCTION_END.search(end_line)
291	        else:
292	            end_line_index, end_line, conjunction = None, None, None
293	        if conjunction:
294	            if end_line_index == index:
295	                finding_line = index + 1
296	                finding_col = start.start("marker") + 1
297	            else:
298	                raw_end_line = next(
299	                    raw for line_index, raw in item_lines
300	                    if line_index == end_line_index
301	                )
302	                masked_end_line = INLINE_CODE.sub(
303	                    lambda match: " " * len(match.group(0)), raw_end_line
304	                )
305	                raw_conjunction = CONJUNCTION_END.search(masked_end_line)
306	                finding_line = end_line_index + 1
307	                finding_col = raw_conjunction.start() + 1 if raw_conjunction else 1
308	            findings.append({
309	                "file": filename,
310	                "line": finding_line,
311	                "col": finding_col,
312	                "rule": "dangling-conjunction",
313	                "level": "advisory-free",
314	                "match": end_line,
315	                "message": "List item ends with a coordinating conjunction. Complete the item or join it with the next item.",
316	            })
317	        index = next_index
318	    return findings

321	def lint(text, filename="<stdin>"):
322	    findings = []
323	    words_total = 0
324	    in_fence = False
325	    lines = text.splitlines()
326	    table_cells = _markdown_table_cells(lines)
327	    # first occurrence of each synonym-group member: (group_idx, base) -> (line, col, match)
328	    seen_synonyms = {}
329	    # consecutive prose lines form one block, so wrapped sentences count once
330	    block = []
331	    in_quote = False
332	
333	    def flush():
334	        findings.extend(_long_sentence_findings(block, filename))
335	        block.clear()
336	
337	    for lineno, raw_line in enumerate(lines, 1):
338	        if CODE_FENCE.match(raw_line.strip()):
339	            flush()
340	            in_fence = not in_fence
341	            continue
342	        if in_fence:
343	            continue
344	        segments = table_cells.get(lineno - 1, [(raw_line, 0)])
345	        is_table = (lineno - 1) in table_cells
346	        quote = BLOCKQUOTE_PREFIX.match(raw_line)
347	        is_quote = bool(quote)
348	        # judge block boundaries on the text inside any blockquote prefix
349	        content = raw_line[quote.end():] if quote else raw_line
350	        standalone = STANDALONE_LINE.match(content)
351	        if (is_table or not content.strip() or standalone
352	                or ANY_LIST_ITEM.match(content) or is_quote != in_quote):
353	            flush()
354	        in_quote = is_quote
355	        for segment, source_column in segments:
356	            line = _mask_inline_code(segment)
357	            words_total += len(line.split())
358	            for rule_id, level, pattern, msg in RULES:
359	                for m in pattern.finditer(line):
360	                    if rule_id == "present-perfect" and MODAL_PERFECT_PREFIX.search(
361	                        line[:m.start()]
362	                    ):
363	                        continue
364	                    findings.append({"file": filename, "line": lineno,
365	                                     "col": source_column + m.start() + 1,
366	                                     "rule": rule_id, "level": level,
367	                                     "match": m.group(0), "message": msg})
368	            for gi, group in enumerate(SYNONYM_GROUPS):
369	                for base in group:
370	                    if (gi, base) in seen_synonyms:
371	                        continue
372	                    m = _word_re(base).search(line)
373	                    if m:
374	                        seen_synonyms[(gi, base)] = (
375	                            lineno, source_column + m.start() + 1, m.group(0)
376	                        )
377	            # the blockquote prefix is markup, not words in the sentence
378	            skip = quote.end() if quote and not is_table else 0
379	            if line[skip:].strip():
380	                block.append((lineno, source_column + skip, line[skip:]))
381	            if is_table:
382	                flush()  # each table cell is its own block
383	        if standalone:
384	            flush()
385	    flush()
386	    # synonym rotation: flag each member after the first, at its first occurrence
387	    for gi, group in enumerate(SYNONYM_GROUPS):
388	        present = [(seen_synonyms[(gi, b)], b) for b in group if (gi, b) in seen_synonyms]
389	        if len(present) > 1:
390	            present.sort()  # document order
391	            first_base = present[0][1]
392	            for (lineno, col, match), base in present[1:]:
393	                findings.append({"file": filename, "line": lineno, "col": col,
394	                                 "rule": "synonym-rotation", "level": "advisory-free",
395	                                 "match": match,
396	                                 "message": f"'{base}' and '{first_base}' name the same action. Pick one and use it every time."})
397	    findings.extend(_dangling_conjunction_findings(text, filename))
398	    findings.sort(key=lambda f: (f["line"], f["col"]))
399	    return findings, words_total

621	def _rule_list(value):
622	    rules = {r for r in value.split(",") if r}
623	    unknown = rules - RULE_IDS
624	    if unknown:
625	        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(
626	            f"unknown rule(s): {', '.join(sorted(unknown))}. "
627	            f"Known rules: {', '.join(sorted(RULE_IDS))}")
628	    return rules

632	    try:
633	        n = int(value)

635	        n = -1
636	    if n < 0:
637	        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(f"expected a non-negative integer, got {value!r}")

# Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100)

ASD-STE100 is a controlled-language standard built by the aerospace and defense industry (ASD, the AeroSpace and Defense Industries Association of Europe) to stop maintenance technicians from misreading English instructions. The standard removes the two biggest sources of misreading: words with more than one meaning, and sentences with more than one possible structure.

This skill borrows that same discipline for a different reader: an **AI agent or a downstream system** that has to parse an English string — an error message, a tool description, an inter-agent instruction, a status report — without a human in the loop to resolve ambiguity. If a maintenance technician can misread "close the valve" as an adjective ("the valve that is near") instead of a command, so can a language model.

## When to Use This Skill

- An agent's output (explanation, instruction, log message, tool description) reads as dense, jargon-heavy, or ambiguous.
- Text will be consumed by another agent, a translation pipeline, or a non-native English reader, and misparsing has a real cost.
- You are writing a prompt, system message, or tool description and want to remove ambiguity before a model ever sees it.
- You want a **before/after** comparison showing exactly which rule was violated and how the rewrite fixes it. Ask for it — the default output is the rewritten text alone (see Output Format).

This skill is not for creative or marketing copy — STE is deliberately flat and literal. Do not apply it to text where voice, nuance, or persuasion is the point.

## Two Modes

Pick a mode before rewriting. If the user does not say which, infer it from the text type. Keep the choice internal unless the user asks for the rule table (see Output Format).

**Strict** — procedures, error messages, tool and function descriptions, inter-agent instructions, safety text. Anywhere a wrong reading has a cost. Apply every rule below, including the hard length caps and one-word-one-meaning discipline.

**STE-flavored** — READMEs, PR descriptions, changelogs, explanatory prose. Apply the structural rules in full and treat the lexical rules as advisory (see Core Rewrite Rules for that split). In practice that means keeping the sentence length caps, active voice, simple tenses, no phrasal verbs, no semicolons, no nominalization and no marketing adjectives, while dropping the one-word-one-meaning lockdown: prose needs some range, and a strict rewrite of prose reads as a personality transplant rather than a clarification.

The two modes and the structural/lexical split are the same distinction seen from two directions. The split says which rules this skill can verify without ASD's dictionary. The modes say which of them to enforce for a given kind of text.

## Source and Scope

This skill encodes the **rule categories** of ASD-STE100 Issue 9 (Jan 2025): 53 writing rules across 9 sections covering word choice, grammar, sentence structure, and style, backed by a dictionary of ~900 approved words (one meaning, one part of speech each) and ~1,200 words to avoid with suggested replacements. See `references/writing-rules.md` for the full rule summary and citations.

It does **not** reproduce ASD's ~900-word approved dictionary verbatim. ASD-STE100 is free to obtain, but it is not free to redistribute: Issue 9, page 2 states that "no reproduction or publication of it, in whole or in part, shall be made without the written authority of an officer of ASD," and grants free reproduction rights only to eight listed categories (ASD/AIA/AIAC member associations and their member companies and customers, member-state defence ministries, A4A, airworthiness authorities, and universities and research institutes for educational purposes). This project is in none of them, so the dictionary stays out of this repo.

Instead, this skill applies the *underlying principle* (pick the plainest, most common word available and use it the same way every time) rather than checking against a fixed word list. When exact ASD-approved wording matters (e.g. actual aircraft maintenance documentation), get the standard and check word-by-word against the real dictionary. Request it from the [official downloads page](https://www.asd-ste100.org/STE_downloads.html) — note that this is a request form that emails you a link, not a direct download.

## Core Rewrite Rules

STE's rules divide into two kinds, and this skill can only fully deliver one of them. **Structural rules** are self-contained: they describe sentence shape, and you can apply them from the description alone. **Lexical rules** are defined entirely by the official ~900-word dictionary, which this skill deliberately does not reproduce (see Source and Scope). Without that dictionary, the lexical rules degrade from a checkable standard into a preference for plain words.

Apply the structural rules with confidence. Apply the lexical rules as a direction of travel, and say so in your output rather than implying dictionary compliance you cannot verify.

### Structural rules — apply these

| Rule | Do | Don't |
|---|---|---|
| Active voice | "The agent deletes the file." | "The file is deleted (by the agent)." — unless the actor is genuinely unknown or irrelevant |
| No phrasal verbs (Rule 9.3) | "Remove the panel." / "Start the job." | "Take off the panel." / "Spin up the job." — a two-word verb has meanings the parts do not predict |
| One instruction per sentence | "Open the file. Read line 3." | "Open the file and read line 3, then check if it matches." |
| Sentence length | ≤20 words for instructions/procedures, ≤25 words for descriptions | Long compound/subordinate-clause sentences |
| No semicolons (Rule 8.1) | Split into separate sentences | Any semicolon at all — STE bans the mark outright, not only as a clause join. (Rule 8.1 permits every other standard punctuation mark. The em dash is *not* banned by STE, though it often signals a sentence that should be split.) |
| Noun clusters | ≤3 words stacked as a noun phrase ("fuel pump valve") | 4+ word noun stacks ("high pressure fuel pump inlet valve assembly") |
| No ellipsis | Keep the subject, verb, and article explicit even if it reads longer | Drop words to save space ("Files not backed up will be lost" → ambiguous which files) |
| Keep modality | "The request **may have** failed." stays "may have" | Promote a hedge to a fact ("The request failed.") or invent a certainty the source did not state |
| Paragraph limits | One topic per paragraph, ≤6 sentences | Multi-topic paragraphs |
| Lists for sequences | Use a numbered or bulleted list for 3+ steps or conditions | Bury a sequence inside one prose sentence |

### Lexical rules — direction of travel only

| Rule | Do | Don't | Why it is weaker here |
|---|---|---|---|
| One word, one meaning | Pick one verb for one action and reuse it every time (e.g. always "check", never mix "check"/"verify"/"confirm" for the same action) | Rotate synonyms for the same idea across a document | Consistency within a document is checkable. Which word is the *approved* one is not, without the dictionary. |
| One part of speech per word | "Apply oil to the valve" (oil = noun) | "Oil the valve" (oil = verb) | Whether "oil" is approved as a noun only is a dictionary fact. Prefer the noun form when both read equally well. Do not claim compliance. |
| Verb, not noun (Rule 3.7) | "Analyze the log." | "Perform an analysis of the log." — a noun form of an action makes the sentence longer and hides who acts | Rule 3.7 says "use an **approved** verb to describe an action." Preferring the verb form is safe to apply anywhere. Knowing which verb is the approved one needs the dictionary. |
| Domain terms | Keep necessary technical nouns/verbs, but define them once if not common English (STE allows a project-specific glossary beyond its base dictionary) | Use jargon without ever defining it | The glossary allowance is real STE, but the base dictionary it extends is absent. |

### Simple tenses — apply with one exception

STE permits infinitive, imperative, simple present, simple past, simple future, and past participle as adjective. It excludes present perfect and other compound forms: "we received the report", not "we have received the report".

Aircraft manuals never need present perfect, so the exclusion costs the standard nothing. Other text is not always so lucky. "The job has completed" (and its output is available now) and "the job completed" (at some past point) are different statements, and status text frequently needs the first. **Where the compound form carries information the simple form cannot — current relevance, or a hedge as in "may have failed" — keep it and flag the departure.** Elsewhere, follow the rule.

## Scan Checklist

These six habits cover most of what makes machine-written English hard to parse. Each one is mechanical: you can point at the exact word or punctuation mark that breaks the rule, with no judgment call. Scan for all six before you rewrite anything.

1. **Synonym rotation** — the same thing gets several names in one document ("the user", "the customer", "the client"). The reader cannot tell whether they are one thing or three. Fix: pick one name, use it every time.
2. **Hedge stacking** — helper verbs and qualifiers pile up until the sentence asserts nothing ("it is important to note that this may potentially help to improve"). Fix: state the claim, or delete it.
3. **Nominalization** — an action frozen into a noun ("perform an analysis of", "provides assistance to"). Fix: use the verb ("analyze", "helps").
4. **Marketing adjectives** — words that claim quality instead of showing it: seamless, robust, powerful, cutting-edge, effortless, blazing-fast. Fix: delete, or replace with the measurement that earns the claim.
5. **Run-on sentences** — several ideas joined by semicolons or em dashes. Fix: one idea per sentence.
6. **Soft phrasal verbs** — spin up, reach out, dive into, kick off. Fix: use the single plain verb (start, contact, read, begin).

## Process

1. Pick the mode (Strict or STE-flavored). Say which only when the user asked for the rule table — see Output Format.
2. Read the input text once for meaning — do not start rewriting before you understand what it must still say afterward.
3. Walk it sentence by sentence. Flag every rule violation from the Core Rewrite Rules tables and every habit from the Scan Checklist. In STE-flavored mode, flag the lexical rules but do not enforce them. For a mechanical first pass over the structural rules, run `scripts/ste-lint.py` (stdin or file args, `--json` for structured output); it checks semicolons, sentence length, phrasal verbs, nominalization, marketing adjectives, synonym rotation, dangling-conjunction in supported list items, passive voice, and compound tenses, and by design never flags hedges or modality. `--baseline N` tolerates N hard violations (for adopting on existing docs); `--disable rule1,rule2` silences named rules.
4. Rewrite each flagged sentence to fix the violation while preserving the original meaning exactly. If a rewrite would drop necessary precision (a safety condition, a scope qualifier, a number), keep the longer phrasing and flag it instead of silently simplifying.
   - **Check modality before you commit to a rewrite.** Hedges ("may", "could", "sometimes", "is likely to") carry the author's confidence, and confidence is content. A shorter sentence that upgrades a hedge to a fact is not a simplification — it is a different claim. This is the most common way a well-intentioned STE rewrite goes wrong, because hedges are exactly what a length cap tempts you to cut.
   - Never add a fact the source did not state. A rewrite that reads better because it supplies a cause, a frequency, or a mechanism has stopped being a rewrite.
5. Output the rewritten text (see Output Format). Keep the mode choice and the rule analysis internal unless the user asked to see them.
6. If the input already complies, say so — do not force changes onto compliant text.

## Output Format

**Default: the rewritten text, and nothing else.** Most callers want a result they can paste straight into a tool description, an error string, or a prompt. Print the simplified text on its own. Do not add a preamble about this skill, a mode announcement, a violation count, a summary of what changed, a rule table, or a closing offer to explain further.

The one permitted addition: if step 4 kept a longer phrasing on purpose, add a single line after the text, prefixed `Kept as-is:`, naming the phrase and the precision that would have been lost. Omit the line when there is nothing to report.

**On request: the rule table.** When the user asks to see the reasoning — "show the diff", "which rules did it break", "explain the changes", "before/after" — output this table instead:

```markdown
| Rule violated | Original | Simplified |
|---|---|---|
| Present perfect tense | "We have received your request." | "We received your request." |
| Noun cluster (4+ words) | "the agent task queue priority handler" | "the handler that sets task-queue priority" |

Mode: Strict. 7 violations found.
```

Follow the table with a one-line note on anything you deliberately did **not** simplify, and why (usually: simplifying would lose required precision).

## Boundaries

**Will:**
- Rewrite ambiguous or dense English into short, single-meaning, active-voice sentences.
- Return the rewritten text alone by default, and name the rules it applied when the user asks.
- Preserve every fact, condition, and scope qualifier in the original.
- Preserve the strength of every hedge, and add no claim the source did not make.
- Suggest a one-line glossary entry for domain terms that must stay.

**Will not:**
- Reproduce ASD's official ~900-word dictionary as if it were memorized verbatim — always treat the official download as the source of truth for exact approved wording.
- Simplify creative, marketing, or persuasive copy where voice and nuance are the point.
- Silently drop a safety condition, exception, or scope qualifier to shorten a sentence — it will flag the trade-off instead.
- Convert "may have failed" into "failed", or "could be caused by X" into "X is the cause" — losing a hedge changes the claim.
- Guarantee an aerospace/defense-grade STE-compliant document. This is a general-purpose clarity tool inspired by STE, not a certified STE authoring tool.
- Make weak content true or useful. STE fixes the *form* of a text, not its substance. A hollow paragraph rewritten under these rules becomes a clean, short, well-punctuated hollow paragraph. If the text has nothing to say, no rewrite fixes that — say so instead of polishing it.
- Shorten past the point of clarity. Cutting words is not the goal. Removing ambiguity is the goal. Past a certain point compression starts costing the reader time rather than saving it, so stop when the sentence is unambiguous, not when it is shortest.

## Additional Resources

- **`references/writing-rules.md`** — fuller summary of the 9 rule sections and dictionary structure, with citations to the official standard and secondary sources.
- **`examples/before-after.md`** — worked examples, including official STE examples and agent-output examples built for this skill.
- **`scripts/ste-lint.py`** — deterministic, stdlib-only linter for the structural rules, including dangling-conjunction in supported list items, plus a synonym-rotation check (one word, one meaning) scoped per file. Exit 1 when hard violations exceed `--baseline` (default 0); advisory findings (passive voice, compound tenses) never fail the run; `--disable` silences named rules. It never flags hedges or modality: those are content, not style, and `--selftest` asserts that "may have failed" passes clean.

Tightening has a floor. A relative tolerance is only reachable if the residual it implies sits
   above the round-off floor of the converged solve. Per-variable checks such as
   `ReferenceResidualConvergence` make this easy to violate: a variable with a tiny reference
   residual turns `nl_rel_tol` into an absolute target far below machine-precision residual
   levels. The signature is a residual that drops normally and then plateaus at a fixed level
   while the solve keeps iterating to `nl_max_its`, and a time stepper that then cuts dt to
   `dtmin`. The fix is an `nl_abs_tol` above that plateau, not a tighter relative tolerance.

input.old_string:
A failure that appears on one CI machine and not on yours cannot be reproduced by rerunning, but
its sensitivity can be. Run several copies of the same input, perturbing one parameter that feeds
the solve by a few units in the 13th significant digit (e.g. a source magnitude or a material
fraction scaled by `1 + k * 1e-13`, `k = 0..7`). That is the size of the difference a different
compiler, CPU or reduction order makes. Run at least four members, and more when the earlier ones
agree, since a small ensemble can agree by chance.

- **As a reproducer.** If members disagree in the quantity the test compares, the test is
  sensitive to rounding, and some member usually reproduces the remote failure. Diffing their
  solver logs locates the first solve where they part, which the remote log alone cannot show.
- **As the acceptance test for a fix.** A fix is robust when every member produces the same
  output to round-off. Fewer failed solves, or a closer match to one member, is not the criterion:
  a change that reduces failures but leaves members disagreeing has moved the instability without
  removing it.
- **For sizing tolerances afterward.** The spread across members of a fixed run is the measured
  noise floor that any remaining tolerance has to clear.

Check that the perturbation actually reaches the solve (members differ in the residual history),
and keep the ensemble short (e.g. the first segment of a transient containing the sensitive solves)
while iterating on candidate fixes. Confirm the chosen fix on the full run.

In a transient with an adaptive time stepper, a nonlinear solve that sometimes converges and
sometimes exhausts `nl_max_its` makes the whole time-step history depend on rounding. Signatures
that distinguish this from an ill-conditioned linear system:

- The linear solves converge to round-off on every iteration, so the matrix is not the problem.
- The nonlinear residual cycles: the same short sequence of values repeats until `nl_max_its`.
- With a variational inequality solver (`vinewtonrsls`), `-snes_vi_monitor` shows the active set
  alternating between the same configurations each cycle. The reduced-space method switches
  constraints on and off discontinuously, so a last-digit difference can decide which side of a
  switch a Newton step lands on.

Tighter tolerances, direct factorizations, and changing the bound value or `nl_max_its` do not
help here, because each cycling solve already reaches the same impasse. Remove what drives the
cycling instead, then judge the result with a perturbation ensemble. Which change works is
case-specific, so try more than one:

- Damping the Newton step with a line search (e.g. `l2`), which stops the full step from
  overshooting into the alternate active set.
- Removing the extrapolated initial guess of a `Predictor` (`Executioner/Predictor/scale=0`), when
  that guess starts solves on the far side of a constraint switch.

its sensitivity can be. Run several copies of the same input, perturbing one parameter that feeds
the solve by a few units in the 13th significant digit (e.g. a source magnitude or a material
fraction scaled by `1 + k * 1e-13`, `k = 0..7`). That is the size of the difference a different
compiler, CPU or reduction order makes. Run at least four members, and more when the earlier ones
agree, since a small ensemble can agree by chance.

  sensitive to rounding, and some member usually reproduces the remote failure. Diffing their
  solver logs locates the first solve where they part, which the remote log alone cannot show.

  output to round-off. Fewer failed solves, or a closer match to one member, is not the criterion:
  a change that reduces failures but leaves members disagreeing has moved the instability without
  removing it.
- **For sizing tolerances afterward.** The spread across members of a fixed run is the measured
  noise floor that any remaining tolerance has to clear.

I installed the asd-ste100 skill and rewrote the new skill prose to follow it. The linter is clean on what I added, except two findings in a sentence that was already there before my edits (below).

**Install:** I used the README's "Clone" method, not `npx skills add`, which would add the skill only to the current TMAP8 project and sends telemetry. Before installing I read everything that would end up loaded or run:
- `README.md`, `SKILL.md` and `scripts/ste-lint.py`, which is stdlib-only, makes no network calls and only reads the files you pass it.
- `references/` and `examples/`, which contain no instructions or commands.

It's now at `~/.claude/skills/asd-ste100` (commit `3944283`), the linter's `--selftest` passes, and the skill is available in this session.

**Rewrite (STE-flavored mode, the one the skill prescribes for explanatory docs):**
- **Long sentences:** I split all 11 sentences over the 25-word cap. Some groups of conditions became short bulleted lists, such as the three-part signature for an unreachable tolerance.
- **Semicolons:** I removed all 3 from the civet-ci-failures additions.
- **Wording:**
  - "robust" in my perturbation section is gone.
  - "has moved" became present tense.
  - I changed one "Remove" to "Delete", because the file already uses "deletes" for the same action.

content.text:
I've narrowed down the contact Jacobian failure from CI data, but haven't reproduced it locally yet. The val-2f suite is still using all 4 CPU slots, so I'll build contact once it finishes.

- **#33833 caused it:** `nodal_normal_derivatives.tri6_penalty_jacobian` passes on the current `next` head (`58160d9b`, Modules job 4280114). The PR doesn't touch `modules/contact`, so the likely cause is the PETSc 3.26 or libMesh update the PR brings in.
- **How it fails** (job 4284953, PETSc 3.26.0): ‖J−Jfd‖/‖J‖ = 1.70e-3, ‖J−Jfd‖ = 9.04, against the spec's `ratio_tol = 6.4e-4` and `difference_tol = 3.1`. Both are about 3× over.
- **Where the tolerances came from:** they were tuned on 2026-10-15, so this test's margin is thin.
- **The DegenerateMap error is a red herring:** the "negative Jacobian" message is the forced Newton step inverting an element after the Jacobian check is done. The spec comment says this abort is expected.
- **What the logs can't tell me:** CI only records the ratio when the test fails, so I don't know what devel's passing ratio is.

Plan once the CPUs free up:
1. **Build:** build the contact module against both stacks, the current PETSc 3.25 and the PETSc 3.26 tree from #33833.
2. **Compare:** run the test on each and record ‖J−Jfd‖/‖J‖. That tells me whether 3.26 moved the hand-coded Jacobian or only the finite-difference one, or whether devel was already close to the tolerance.
3. **Locate:** use `-snes_test_jacobian_view` to find which blocks differ. Contact-to-bulk or friction blocks would point to a real Jacobian bug. Changes spread across the matrix would point to the FD step or a sparsity effect, since the spec mentions #34065.

I'll report what I find before changing the spec or the code.
